inline.s: [From this the bhikshu fell into wrong views and no longer advanced in practice. He himself thought he had realized the great Way, and so went from delusion into delusion, sunk in the long night. Pity the beings! Seeking the Way without encountering a true good friend, one cannot but fall into the snare — how can one not be careful! Now you should know that, because of the wrong view of the past, you obtained the retribution of the five outflows
Because you lost right knowledge, you again met an evil teacher, whose poison-sting
shì
you personally suffered — how can you not arouse fear? Now you should quickly arouse right faith, and with all your mind remember Amitabha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.']

From this the bhikshu fell into wrong views and no longer advanced in practice. He thought he had already realized the great Way, and so went from delusion into delusion, sunk in the long night. How pitiable are beings! Seeking the Way without encountering a true good friend, one cannot but fall into the snare of wrong views — how can one not be vigilant! Now you should know that, owing to the wrong view of the past, you felt the retribution of transmigrating through the five paths. Because you lost right knowledge, you again met an evil teacher and personally suffered his poison-harming — how can you not arouse fear? Now you should quickly arouse right faith, and with all your mind think on Amitabha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.'

[The five outflows] Here it refers to the five paths that have outflows. 'Outflow' is another name for afflictions. [The five paths] These are the places where afflicted beings come and go, hence called 'paths.' There are five: one, the hell path; two, the hungry-ghost path; three, the animal path; four, the human path; five, the heaven path.
Question: Since 'all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha,' what need is there to practice?
Answer: 'All dharmas are empty and still' means that all dharmas are empty of anything at all, still without arising or ceasing. The whole ten Dharma-realms are a single dream of ignorance
(see
The Real Nature of All Dharmas
article)

, so all dharmas are illusions, empty of anything at all, still without arising or ceasing. 'My mind is the Buddha' is what is commonly called 'this very mind is the Buddha.' Here 'mind' refers to self-nature, while the 'mind' of body-and-mind refers to the function of self-nature. The meaning of 'this very mind is the Buddha' is: the Buddha is nothing other than the mind (self-nature). And in essence, the self-nature of the Buddhas and the self-nature of sentient beings are entirely the same; only, the Buddhas' self-nature is aware, while sentient beings' self-nature is deluded.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: 'When self-nature is deluded, that is sentient beings; when self-nature is aware, that is the Buddha.' (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha

article.) Practice is meant to turn self-nature from delusion to awareness, from sentient being to Buddha. Therefore one must practice in order to leave the cycle of rebirth and to realize Buddhahood.
[The ten Dharma-realms]
Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary; the last four are the four noble.

[Wu Xiu asked on behalf of a friend how long his life would be. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse, saying: 'Human life is like the morning dew, floating and unsettled, with no fixed time; unable to escape the dream and illusion, why must one seek to know beforehand?' He further revealed: 'Do not for him ask the date; when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you may be sure he will be in a fluster.' This friend indeed died of illness on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the following year. When Wu Xiu heard this, he sought instruction.]

Wu Xiu asked on behalf of a friend how long his life-span would be. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'Human life is like the morning dew, floating and unsettled, with no fixed time; unable to escape the dream and illusion, why must one seek to know beforehand?' He further revealed: 'Do not for him ask the date of his death; when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month comes, be sure he will be in a fluster.' This friend indeed fell ill and died on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the following year. When Wu Xiu heard this news, he sought instruction from the Bodhisattva.

[The Bodhisattva said: 'Yuan Bo, you should know that studying the Way without understanding this mind is like building a house without a foundation, or crossing a river without a raft. One who wishes to understand the mind should minutely investigate: this body and this mind — from what do they arise? Since the four great elements are illusory, where is the mind to be lodged? Body and mind being illusory, the world and its dust-particles are without the slightest difference. The myriad dharmas before one's eyes — from where do they arise? From where do they cease? If there is no arising and ceasing, then the illuminating and that which is illuminated both have nothing to rely on, and of itself one sees the ground of True Thusness' extinction and peace.']

The Bodhisattva said: 'Yuan Bo, you should know that studying the Way without understanding this mind is like building a house without a foundation, or crossing a river without a boat. To understand the mind, you must minutely investigate: this body and this mind — from what do they arise? Since the four great elements (here referring to the body) are illusory, on what will the mind rely? Therefore the mind too is illusory. Having understood that body and mind are illusory, then the whole world and a single particle of dust are without the slightest difference, for they are all illusions. Then, further contemplate: the myriad dharmas before one's eyes — from where do they arise? To where do they pass away? If they are without arising and ceasing (illusions naturally have no arising or ceasing), then the illuminating and the illuminated both have nothing to rely on, and of itself one will see the ground of True Thusness' extinction and peace, directly realizing that birth and death are illusory.'
[The four great elements]

The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. Earth has the nature of hardness, water of moisture, fire of warmth, and wind of motion. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures — hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion — and so they are called 'great.' For example, the hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, flesh, and sinews of a human body are the hard earth element; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, phlegm, tears, urine, and excrement are the moist water element; warmth and heat are the warm fire element; and the in-and-out of one breath is the moving wind element.

[Where is the mind to be lodged?] Here 'mind' refers to the shadows of the six sense-objects. [The shadows of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced by the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects, and these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, hence they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom images of conditioning on the six sense-objects. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: 'What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time, all beings have all manner of inversion, like a person who is lost and mistakes the four directions; falsely taking the four great elements as their own form, and the shadows of the six sense-objects as their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; the sick one falsely grasps them. Because of this false grasping, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of this sky, but he is also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this there is falsely the transmigration of birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.' (Translation: What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time, all beings have had all manner of inversion, taking the false as real, and this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his way, mistaking north for south and east for west; falsely taking the body formed of the four great elements as the substance of self, and the thoughts arising from the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects as the substance of mind. It is like eyes that are dazzled, falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; these are phantoms falsely grasped by a diseased eye. Because of false grasping, one not only falsely grasps the emptiness of the sky as real, but also thinks real flowers truly arise from it. Because beings, through the inversion and delusion of not comprehending, falsely take the illusory body and mind as real and cling to them as self, they thereupon transmigrate in birth and death, and so this is called ignorance.)

[Kong Sheng of Gouqu had kept a vegetarian diet for twenty years. Thinking of his own aging, he asked: 'What is there after death?' And wept without cease. The Bodhisattva said: 'You need not shed sorrowful tears; just follow what I say, deeply believe and practice it, and after death you will naturally have a good place to settle your body.' Thereupon he bestowed a verse: 'In the West there is a Pure Land, where humans and devas alike take refuge; if you can cultivate this gate, secure
(the same as 'wen' — still and secure)
without fear or doubt.']

Kong Sheng of Gouqu had maintained a vegetarian diet for twenty years. Thinking of his own aging, he asked the Bodhisattva: 'What will there be after death?' Thereupon he wept without cease. The Bodhisattva instructed: 'You need not weep in sorrow; only follow what I say, deeply believe and practice it, and after your life ends you will naturally have a good place to dwell.' Thereupon he gave him a verse: 'In the West there is a Pure Land, where humans and devas alike take refuge; if you can cultivate this gate, secure and at peace, without fear or doubt.'

[Shen Wenzhou was celebrated for his mastery of cold-damage, and had just arrived to pay respects. The Bodhisattva asked: 'When cold enters the pericardium, what illness is that?' He answered: 'It is called cold-stroke
zhòng hán,
illness caused by catching cold)

.' Thereupon, as an illustration for the assembly, he said: 'You only know that when cold enters the pericardium, it is called the illness of cold-stroke. But if a wrong enters the mind, that is an illness that costs one his life! You people take only a bodily illness as an illness and promptly regulate and cure it; yet when the mind has a great illness, you do not consult a bright physician, do not seek a wondrous medicine, and let it suffer its pain without awareness — alas!']

Shen Wenzhou was a master proficient in the Treatise on Cold-Damage, and had just arrived to pay respects to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva asked: 'When cold enters the pericardium, what illness is that?' Shen Wenzhou answered: 'This is cold-stroke (
zhòng hán

, illness caused by catching cold).' Thereupon the Bodhisattva instructed the assembly: 'You only know that when cold enters the pericardium, one gets the illness of cold-stroke. But if a wrong enters the mind, that is a fatal illness! You people take only a bodily illness as an illness and immediately regulate and cure it; but when the mind has a great illness, you do not consult a bright physician, do not seek a wondrous medicine, and let it suffer its pain without awareness — how sorrowful!'

[Treatise on Cold-Damage] The earliest work in existing Chinese medicine that systematically discusses externally-contracted disease. Ten volumes in all. Written by Zhang Zhongjing of the Eastern Han in the

rd century. It established the six-channel syndrome differentiation and principles of treatment, and the combination of prescriptions; in diagnosis it threads together the four examinations and the eight guiding principles.

[Chen Daxin followed the teaching and recited the Buddha's name with the utmost sincerity. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse, saying: 'In the pool of the eight virtues a lotus has already been planted; indeed a single thought is most profound and deep. Though its watering and nurture rely on the Tathagata's power, its growth depends entirely on a mind of resolve.' He further addressed the assembly: 'In this land, when one makes the vow to be reborn, then in that land a lotus immediately grows. Therefore he spoke thus; you should arouse deep faith.']

Chen Daxin followed the Bodhisattva's teaching and recited the Buddha's name with the utmost sincerity. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'In the pool of the eight virtues (the pool filled with the water of the eight virtues) a lotus has already been planted; indeed a single thought is most profound and deep. Though its watering and nurture rely on the Tathagata's power, its growth depends entirely on a mind of resolve.' He further instructed the assembly: 'In this land, the moment one makes the vow to be reborn, in that land (the Land of Ultimate Bliss) a lotus at once grows. So my verse says "in the pool of the eight virtues a lotus has already been planted"; you should arouse deep faith.'

[The water of the eight virtues] In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a pool of the seven jewels, filled with the water of the eight virtues. This water has eight kinds of supreme virtue: one, pure and clear; two, cool and refreshing; three, sweet and fine; four, light and soft; five, moistening and enriching; six, peaceful and harmonious; seven, when drunk, it removes thirst, hunger, and countless other ills; eight, after drinking, it is certain to nourish the faculties and the four great elements, and to increase all manner of supreme wholesome roots.

blocks.text: Fond of the Art of Elixir

inline.s: [Sun Zhongbai was fond of the art of elixir; after long practice it was ineffective, so he came to the gathering to pay respects. The Bodhisattva rebuked him, saying: 'Old baldhead, today you have changed this look to come see me? Let me ask you: when can your gold elixir be completed?' He answered: 'I am precisely seeking its completion.' The Bodhisattva said: 'If it is completed, be sure to keep several pellets; do not eat them all into your belly. Wait until
sì
wait)
you see old Yama, so that you may make a gift to present. Foolish old man, this matter truly has no share for you; it is better to return to what you ought to do.' Sun bowed and thanked him.']

Sun Zhongbai was fond of the art of alchemy; after long practice it proved ineffective, so he came to the gathering and paid respects to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva rebuked him: 'Old baldhead, today you have changed your visage to see me? Let me ask you: when can your gold elixir be completed?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'I have precisely come to ask you to help me complete it.' The Bodhisattva said: 'If it is completed, be sure to keep several pellets; do not swallow them all into your belly. When you meet old Yama, you can use them as a gift to present to him, begging him to spare you. Foolish old man, the matter of refining the elixir and becoming an immortal surely has no share for you; it is better to do what you ought to do (the task that falls within your proper lot).' Sun Zhongbai bowed and thanked the Bodhisattva for his instruction.
[The art of elixir]

It includes both the 'external elixir' and the 'internal elixir.' The external elixir uses cinnabar (red mercuric sulfide) along with lead, sulfur, and other ingredients, refined into a yellow medicinal gold whose product is called the gold elixir. Daoism holds that after taking it one can become a transcendent and never age. The gold elixir mostly refers to the external elixir, but also to the internal elixir that one refines — taking the body as a 'furnace and vessel,' using the 'essence' and 'breath' within the body as the medicine, and refining by means of 'spirit.' Daoism holds that causing essence, breath, and spirit to congeal can form a 'holy embryo,' whereby one can shed the body and be reborn as a transcendent.
[Gifts]
Presents intended as offerings.

[After a while, the Bodhisattva again said: 'Foolish old man, do you know your own proper lot?' He answered: 'Seeking to see my nature is my proper lot.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Do you know this nature — is it great or small, blue or yellow?' He answered: 'Nature has no such marks.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Then where do you wish to seek to see it?' Sun had no reply, and so aroused faith and took refuge, wishing to be a disciple and asking for a Dharma name. Thereupon he revealed a verse for him, saying: 'Nature has no marks of great or small, blue or yellow; how can there be a name for you to call? If one does not reach the profound mystery of this, every word and half a phrase is confusion.']

After a while, the Bodhisattva again said: 'Foolish old man, do you know your own proper lot?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'I seek to see my nature; this is my proper lot.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Do you know this nature — is it great or small (in form), blue or yellow (in color)?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'Nature has no such marks.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Since it has no marks, then where do you wish to seek to see it?' Sun Zhongbai could not answer, and so aroused faith and took refuge in the Bodhisattva, wishing to be his disciple and asking him to bestow a Dharma name. Thereupon the Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'Nature has no marks of great or small, blue or yellow; how can there be a name for you to call? If one does not reach the profound mystery of this, every word and half a phrase is confusion (a mistake).'

['I now forcibly establish a name for you; you may be called Da Ben. After this, your remaining time will not amount to seven or eight years — do not squander the thirty-six years of ascetic practice of eight hundred years ago!' Sun then asked how this body would come to an end. The Bodhisattva said: 'An end is an end; why ask again how it will end?' Sun then asked how to practice. The Bodhisattva said: 'The gate of the Pure Land can broadly gather beings of all types. You ask about practice — you should be mindful of Amitabha Buddha, make the vow to be reborn there, then all will be settled once and for all; be no more deluded.']

I now give you the name Da Ben. After this, your life-span will not exceed seven or eight years; do not in any way squander the thirty-six years of ascetic practice of eight hundred years ago!' Sun Zhongbai thereupon asked how this body would come to an end. The Bodhisattva said: 'An end is an end; why ask moreover how it will end?' Sun Zhongbai then asked: 'How should one practice?' The Bodhisattva said: 'The gate of the Pure Land can broadly gather beings of all faculties. You ask about practice — you should be mindful of Amitabha Buddha and make the vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and then you will have everything settled once and for all; be deluded no longer.'
[I forcibly establish a name for you] Dharms are originally without name, so to establish this name is called 'forcibly doing so.'

[Then all is settled once and for all] Sun Zhongbai's goal was to see his nature and attain awakening; the Bodhisattva taught him to recite the Buddha, because 'once one sees Amitabha, why worry about not awakening?' Hence he said: 'then one settles everything once and for all.'
